title: Participation Is Not Collaboration: Tracing Public Ownership After Cross-Product Agent Review
description:
Reproducible analysis artifact for the EMSE 2026 Special Issue paper "Participation Is Not Collaboration: Tracing Public Ownership After Cross-Product Agent Review".

Context. A pull request written by one coding-agent product and reviewed by another looks like a multi-agent workflow. Two products on one pull request do not show that one addressed the other. Objective. We trace the public path from cross-product review to an addressed edge, a next owner, and a later state. Method. From a pinned AIDev release we analyse 8,608 trigger pull requests, 546 matched pairs, and a 1,067-PR outcome cohort. Exact account, comment, and review-batch identifiers anchor every event to one trigger. We set aside automation bursts, fix an hour-48 check point, and test the exposure against placebo anchors. Results. Direct dialogue between products is rare; after a five-minute burst, user accounts own most remaining first actions. Cross-product triggers get 13 percentage points less visible follow-up than matched same-product triggers. An exact reply to the trigger goes with 17 points more later merge, and a person writes it four times in five. Placebo exposures then qualify it: a reply anchored anywhere else on the pull request does as well, and shuffling the anchor leaves the estimate unmoved. Across all 105 user-written replies, the association sits with the ones a person wrote, not the one-click hand-offs to another machine. Naming an issue in the pull request body roughly doubles the chance a review point is answered across the boundary, and changes nothing within a product. Conclusions. Report public multi-agent impact as a map of connections, not a count of products. The trace shows retained human attention, not a resolved review point, and strict anchoring buys attribution rather than prediction.

What this archive contains. The analysis and figure code, the reproduction contract and protocol ledgers, the test suite, the licence files, the README, the citation metadata, and the derived analysis products under outputs/ that the manuscript tables and figures are built from.

What this archive deliberately excludes. The AIDev-7.6M release itself, which is third-party data under its own terms and has its own home; the pinned revision is recorded here and in the code so a user can fetch exactly the same one. Also excluded, and asserted on at build time, are the private coder keys and answer keys that would de-blind the human-coding audits, the author-metadata audit, ad-hoc exploration scratch, and the submission-portal staging folder.

Licence scope. The MIT licence covers the analysis code, figure code, build scripts, and the derived analysis products. It does not cover the AIDev-7.6M release or any other third-party dataset screened during the external-evidence audit, nor the manuscript text and figures, whose rights transfer is governed by the publisher agreement.
